'''George Algis Paulikas''' (born May 14, 1936) is an American [[physicist]], [[space scientist]], and science administrator best known for his pioneering contributions to the study of Earth's [[magnetosphere]] and energetic particles in near-Earth space, as well as for senior leadership roles at [[The Aerospace Corporation]] and extensive post-retirement service to the [[National Academies of Sciences]], Engineering, and Medicine. He worked at The Aerospace Corporation for 37 years, rising from technical staff scientist to executive vice president and contributing to U.S. national security and civil space programs.

Paulikas has been recognized as a Fellow of the [[American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics]] (AIAA)<ref>{{cite web |title=AIAA Fellows |url=https://aiaa.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/AIAA-Fellow-Roster_2025.pdf |website=aiaa.org}}</ref> and the [[American Physical Society]] (APS) and is a recipient of the [[National Reconnaissance Office]] (NRO) Gold Medal for Technical Excellence and Leadership.

== Early life and education ==
Paulikas was born in [[Pagėgiai]], Lithuania, in 1936 and immigrated to the [[United States]] with his family in 1949, settling in [[Chicago]]. He earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[Engineering physics|Engineering Physics]] (1957) and a Master of Science in physics (1958) from the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|University of Illinois]], followed by a Ph.D. in physics (1961) from the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{cite web |title=George Paulikas |url=https://grainger.illinois.edu/alumni/distinguished/George-Paulikas |website=University of Illinois Grainger College of Engineering}}</ref>

At Berkeley, his doctoral research was conducted in laboratory plasma physics under the supervision of [[Wulf Bernard Kunkel]], a physicist noted for contributions to [[plasma diagnostics]] and [[fusion research]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=George Paulikas papers - Archives West |url=https://archiveswest.orbiscascade.org/ark:80444/xv497264 |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=archiveswest.orbiscascade.org}}</ref>

== Career ==
Paulikas joined [[The Aerospace Corporation]] in 1961, the year he completed his doctorate, beginning as a member of the technical staff. He spent 37 years with the organization, holding roles including department head, laboratory director, vice president, senior vice president, and executive vice president.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1981-04-05 |title=George Paulikas, 1981, Los Angeles, California |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times-george-paulikas-1/29453544/ |access-date=2026-02-24 |work=The Los Angeles Times |pages=229}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=We Hear That |url=https://aip.brightspotcdn.com/PTO.v21.i11.115_1.online.pdf |website=physicstoday.aip.org}}</ref>

=== Scientific contributions ===
During the early phase of his career, Paulikas was a contributor to the measurement and interpretation of energetic charged particles in Earth's magnetosphere. His work significantly advanced understanding of space radiation dynamics and their effects on spacecraft systems. A seminal 1979 paper co-authored with J. B. Blake became a foundational reference in [[magnetospheric physics]] and was later revisited by scientists involved in [[NASA]]’s Van Allen Probes mission (2012–2019).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pieters |first1=Carle M. |last2=Paulikas |first2=George A. |title=Radiation belts revisited |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/450610b |journal=Nature |date=November 2007 |volume=450 |issue=7170 |pages=610 |doi=10.1038/450610b |pmid=18046377 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

As a principal investigator and later director of the Space Sciences Laboratory, Paulikas led multiple satellite instrumentation experiments sponsored by the U.S. Air Force, supporting both space science research and the design of spacecraft able to operate in high-radiation environments.<ref>{{Cite web |title=George Paulikas|url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11416/chapter/12 |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=nationalacademies.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Science could soar with world's most powerful rocket |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn16128-science-could-soar-with-worlds-most-powerful-rocket/ |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=New Scientist |language=en-US}}</ref>

From the late 1960s, Paulikas focused primarily on science and engineering management. In senior administrative roles, he oversaw changes to corporate research funding, directed studies on advanced space systems, and supervised the development and operation of specialized space systems for U.S. national security. He retired in 1998.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Dychtwald |first1=Ken |last2=Erickson |first2=Tamara J. |last3=Morison |first3=Robert |date=2004-03-01 |title=It's Time to Retire Retirement |url=https://hbr.org/2004/03/its-time-to-retire-retirement |access-date=2026-02-24 |work=Harvard Business Review |language=en |issn=0017-8012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |title=A Lunar To-Do List |journal=Science |date=2006 |volume=313 |issue=5794 |page=1715 |doi=10.1126/science.313.5794.1715b}}</ref>

== Service to the National Academies ==
After retiring, Paulikas became involved in advisory and governance work with the [[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine]]. He served as vice chair of the National Research Council’s Space Studies Board from 2003 to 2006 and participated in multiple study committees on U.S. space policy, exploration strategy, and science program priorities.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Scientific Context for Exploration of the Moon |url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11954/chapter/17 |website=National Academies Press}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |title=A Lunar To-Do List |journal=Science |date=2006 |volume=313 |issue=5794 |page=1715 |doi=10.1126/science.313.5794.1715b}}</ref>

He also chaired the committee that produced ''The Scientific Context for Exploration of the Moon'' (2007), which outlined scientific objectives for lunar exploration and informed planning at NASA.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11954/chapter/1 |title=The Scientific Context for Exploration of the Moon (2007) |language=en}}</ref>

His committee work additionally included assessments of NASA’s science programs, systems integration for the Constellation program, Earth science strategy, and the future of the U.S. civil space program.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thomas |first=George Paulikas, Kathryn Thornton, Greg |date=2008-05-12 |title=COMMENTARY: Constellation Capabilities and Science |url=https://spacenews.com/commentary-constellation-capabilities-and-science/ |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=SpaceNews |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Far side could be ideal for radio observatory |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn12019-far-side-could-be-ideal-for-radio-observatory/ |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=New Scientist |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Honors and recognition ==

* Trustees’ Distinguished Achievement Award, The Aerospace Corporation (1981), the organization's highest internal honor, awarded for research on space radiation effects<ref>{{cite news |title=George Paulikas honored |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/29453544/george_paulikas_1981_los_angeles/ |work=Los Angeles Times}}</ref>
* U.S. Air Force Meritorious Civilian Service Award (1981)
* U.S. Air Force Space Division Excellence Award (1984)
* National Reconnaissance Office Gold Medal for Technical Excellence and Leadership
* Fellow, American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics
* Fellow, American Physical Society

He is also honored on the [[Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum]] Wall of Honor as an Air and Space Leader.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. George Paulikas |url=https://airandspace.si.edu/support/wall-of-honor/dr-george-paulikas |website=Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum}}</ref>

A formal tribute to Paulikas was entered into the [[U.S. Congressional Record]] on July 20, 1999, by Representative [[Steven T. Kuykendall]] (CA) honoring his 50 years in the United States, his professional achievements, and his family's immigration story.<ref>{{cite web |title=Congressional tribute to George A. Paulikas |url=https://hdl.huntington.org/digital/collection/p15150coll7/id/7844/ |website=Huntington Digital Library}}</ref>

Paulikas authored the memoir ''Thirteen Years, 1936–1949'', which documents his early life in Lithuania and his family's immigration to the United States following World War II.<ref>{{cite web |title=Thirteen Years, 1936–1949 |url=http://www.old.lituanus.org/1999/99_1_11.htm |website=Lituanus}}</ref>
